B3:
**B3 — Returns correct shortened string (algorithm)**

Judge this item on the string the method would actually return when the response's code is taken as written, end-to-end: follow the loop bounds, the indices, and the hyphen location the rest of the method produces, then ask whether the method would return the correct shortened string for a typical valid username. No_deduct only if that end-to-end result is correct; deduct if it is not — for example, a response whose loop is bounded by a constant (`i < 10`) or whose index search is off so the final returned string is wrong loses B3 even though its substring/concatenation logic is textbook. Likewise deduct for algorithmic defects in building and returning the string itself: failing to return the string, incorrectly building it (early return, failing to initialize correctly), bounds errors, modifying `username`, or printing instead of (or in addition to) returning.

Do not deduct for faults that are not algorithmic. Malformed String method usage — wrong argument order, wrong number of arguments, or a wrong method name, e.g. `username.substring(i, 0)` or `username.subString(0, i)` — is the excused "calls a String method incorrectly" case, not a disqualifying bounds error, so long as the intended algorithm (which pieces of the string are combined and returned) is correct. Similarly, ignore compilation-level slips elsewhere in the method that are unrelated to the algorithm — an undeclared variable, a missing brace, returning a value whose type is slightly off — whenever the intended construction and return of the correct string is unambiguous.
